newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary electricity suppliers' bad debt to rise.
newsitem.headline: Hungary electricity suppliers' bad debt to rise.

text.p: Hungary's recently privatised electricity distributors will face increasing bad debts when the delayed energy price rise takes place on January 1, analysts said.

The government last month postponed an energy price rise expected for October 1 to January 1, saying the new deadline would still give utilities an eight percent return on equity as stipulated during privatisation.
A government decree said that the price rise, guaranteeing the margin must be carried out on October 1.
However, the long-awaited price rise could prove a mixed blessing as it is also susceptible to increased customer insolvency, an analyst said.
"I think the mismatch between cash inflow and cash outflow will increase," Jerry Hwang, director of international sales with OTP Broker, told Reuters.
He added, that at the moment the utility companies finance a great portion of their customer debt.
"They have to pay suppliers almost immediately, but their customers have a 90-day period before any action can be taken," Hwang said.

One of the privatised electricity suppliers, EMASZ, 48.81 percent owned by the German RWE/EVS consortium has an indebtedness rate of 7.3 percent compared to the company's assets, an OTP Broker report said.
However, another analyst said exactly because of the prospect of rising bad debts, the companies might change their billing procedures.
"All things being equal, delayed payments would rise. But companies are likely to bring some changes in the collection of fees," said Robert Feuer of ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.

Hungary last December sold large stakes in six regional electricity distribution companies and two power stations to Western giants such as RWE of Germany and Electricite de France (EDF) for around $1 billion.
Energy distributors say they have made their 1996 plans based on an October price rise.
The buyers also undertook significant grid modernisation of Hungary's long neglected power distribution system.

"The company needs to carry out large investment because of neglected modernisation in recent years," OTP Broker said in a report about another electricity supplier, TITASZ, adding that virtually the same held true for EMASZ.
Wolfgang Strassburg, head of RWE's Central Division said earlier that 40 billion forints ($267 million) have to be found this year to begin modernisation.
Hwang did not believe the delay in energy price rises would also mean a delay in modernisation.
"There hasn't been a precedent for the government reneging on one of its own decrees . I would hesitate to say that they would offset one failure with another," Hwang said.
"Neither side has the luxury of unilaterally going its own way," Hwang said. "They have to work together."
The exact size of the energy price rise, now expected for January 1, is still unknown, mainly because the government faces a difficult balancing act.
Last month, the government rejected the Industry and Trade Ministry's study upon the increase would have been based and has put Socialist Imre Karl in charge of overviewing it.
He admitted that the energy price rise is not only an economic but a political decision as well.
Inflation in Hungary is expected to be between 22 to 24 percent this year, and an October price increase would have increased that figure.
"Nobody really knows what the balance will be between political feasibility and economic imperatives," Hwang said.
